extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; students and critics of literature, philosophy, and rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing evaluative principles and compositional guidance found in Pascal's Pensées (and T. S. Eliot's introduction) about thought, style, persuasion, and method in literary/philosophical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: mathematical_vs_intuitive_mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the mathematical mind (principles are explicit, suited to axioms/definitions) and the intuitive mind (principles are implicit in common use and perceived at a glance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match method to mental type and audience: do not force mathematical procedure on intuitive subjects or expect intuitive perception from mathematicians. Mathematicians reason rightly when premises are explicit; intuitive minds perceive subtle, numerous principles without formal demonstration. Beware attempting to express intuitive principles by long formal definitions — they must often be shown or felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: right_understanding_varies_by_domain
rubrics_metrics.description: There are different kinds of 'right understanding': some people understand best in domains with few premises and subtle conclusions, others in domains with many premises and structured relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess competence relative to the order of things under discussion (e.g., hydrostatics vs. broad conceptual systems). When evaluating a thinker/writing, note whether the intellect is precise (penetrates few premises deeply) or mathematical (handles many premises comprehensively).

rubrics_metrics.name: intuition_vs_formal_reasoning_in_communication
rubrics_metrics.description: People accustomed to judge by feeling do not naturally follow formal chains of reasoning, and conversely those trained in reasoning may fail to grasp matters perceived by feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating argument or prose, choose forms appropriate to the audience's habitual mode (feeling/intuitive vs. formal/reasoning); do not expect one mode to substitute for the other without support or translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: true_eloquence_is_unobtrusive
rubrics_metrics.description: True eloquence 'makes light of eloquence' — the best style does not call attention to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for naturalness and restraint: style should serve thought and feeling rather than display rhetorical skill. Excessive self-conscious ornamentation undermines the moral and persuasive force of prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: judgment_over_mechanical_rules
rubrics_metrics.description: One should prefer sound judgment to slavish adherence to prescriptive rules when assessing time, feeling, or literary effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules (like a watch) can be useful, but the practiced eye/ear/judgment that adapts to context is superior. Avoid evaluating works solely by rote checklists; value nuanced perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: company_and_intercourse_shape_understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding and feelings are moulded (improved or corrupted) by social intercourse and company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To develop good taste and judgment, choose associations and reading that improve rather than corrupt intellect and sensibility. Evaluators should consider social/contextual influences on an author's outlook and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: correct_with_advantage_by_admitting_their_side
rubrics_metrics.description: When pointing out another's error, first notice and admit the truth in the side from which they view the matter, then reveal where that perspective is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This persuasion technique reduces offence and leads the interlocutor to accept correction because they see their partial truth acknowledged. Useful in critique, pedagogy, and polemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: persuasion_is_self_discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: People are generally better persuaded by reasons they discover themselves than by those presented to them by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure exposition and argument to lead readers toward self-discovery (Socratic/diagnostic methods, prompting reflection) rather than blunt assertion; provide paths for readers to arrive at conclusions to increase acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_overformalizing_intuitive_subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to treat matters of intuition by beginning with definitions and axioms as in mathematics; such formalism repels intuitive minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For subjects where principles are felt rather than demonstrable, present examples, feelable instances, or implicit demonstrations rather than abstract axiomatization. Reserve formal methods for domains where premises are explicit and manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: do_not_cultivate_automatic_writing_as_model
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic or purely inspired writing cannot reliably be cultivated as a method of composition; masterpieces are not produced whole by such inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While moments of sudden composition occur, responsible composition relies on revision, reason, and craft. Do not advise aspiring writers to rely on automatic writing as a repeatable technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: fragmentary_expression_requires_whole_for_understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Pascal's Pensées are fragmentary in expression, but many fragments cannot be detached from the whole; understanding parts requires some grasp of the intended whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or presenting fragmentary or aphoristic writing, assess how fragments function within a broader architecture or program; avoid treating isolated sayings as fully self-contained without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: heart_reasons_are_rational_in_their_own_way
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'heart' (affective perception) has reasons that reason does not know; in Pascal's sense, the heart can be truly rational when it is genuinely the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize emotions and affective judgments as legitimate components of conviction and understanding, especially in theological or moral writing. Do not equate 'heart' with irrationality; evaluate whether affective claims are coherent with the author's whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: three_orders_and_discontinuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the three 'orders' — order of nature, order of mind, and order of charity — as discontinuous; higher orders are not implicit in lower ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reductionist critiques that try to explain moral/spiritual phenomena solely from natural or intellectual domains. When analysing moral or religious texts, respect possible discontinuities and different kinds of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: apologetic_method_by_rejection_and_elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Pascal's apologetic method proceeds by rejecting inadequate non-religious explanations of the world and eliminating alternatives until Christianity (particularly Catholic Christianity) appears most satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing an apology or persuasive philosophical argument, systematically identify and eliminate rival accounts, showing how they fail to account for facts, values, or 'the moral world'; use 'powerful and concurrent' reasons to point toward the preferred position.
